claim: TCOF1 and NOLC1 associate with all subunits of the CK2 kinase.
source: These experiments showed that both NOLC1 and TCOF1 interacted with all subunits of the CK2 kinase (Figure 1A), which was consistent with earlier studies that found these proteins to be phosphorylated by CK2 (Jones et al., 1999; Meier and Blobel, 1992; Wise et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by CompPASS mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1A and confirmed by previous citations showing CK2 phosphorylation of these proteins.

claim: TCOF1 and NOLC1 have been previously found to be phosphorylated by CK2.
source: These experiments showed that both NOLC1 and TCOF1 interacted with all subunits of the CK2 kinase (Figure 1A), which was consistent with earlier studies that found these proteins to be phosphorylated by CK2 (Jones et al., 1999; Meier and Blobel, 1992; Wise et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by three citations to prior published work.

claim: CK2 inhibition prevents NOLC1 and TCOF1 from binding to CUL3KBTBD8.
source: Such effective inhibition of CK2 prevented NOLC1 or TCOF1 from binding to CUL3KBTBD8, whereas PKN1, a protein that associates with a different surface of KBTBD8 and is not important for neural crest specification (Werner et al., 2015), was still recognized (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C using shRNA depletion and small molecule inhibition of CK2.

claim: PKN1 associates with a different surface of KBTBD8 and is not important for neural crest specification.
source: Such effective inhibition of CK2 prevented NOLC1 or TCOF1 from binding to CUL3KBTBD8, whereas PKN1, a protein that associates with a different surface of KBTBD8 and is not important for neural crest specification (Werner et al., 2015), was still recognized (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Inhibition of CK2 blocks CUL3KBTBD8-dependent monoubiquitylation of TCOF1 and NOLC1.
source: Inhibition of CK2 also blocked CUL3KBTBD8-dependent monoubiquitylation of TCOF1 and NOLC1, while the modification of an unrelated protein, PCNA, was not impaired (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1D and 1E using denaturing ubiquitin pulldowns.

claim: Inactivation of PP1 and PP2A phosphatases promotes substrate binding and monoubiquitylation by CUL3KBTBD8.
source: In line with these results, inactivation of PP1 and PP2A phosphatases, which oppose CK2 in cells (Popescu et al., 2009), strongly promoted substrate binding and monoubiquitylation by CUL3KBTBD8 (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 1F and 1G, and by a citation indicating PP1/PP2A oppose CK2.

claim: PP1 and PP2A phosphatases oppose CK2 in cells.
source: In line with these results, inactivation of PP1 and PP2A phosphatases, which oppose CK2 in cells (Popescu et al., 2009), strongly promoted substrate binding and monoubiquitylation by CUL3KBTBD8 (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: The phosphatase subunit PP1A decreases during neural crest specification in vitro.
source: Interestingly, the phosphatase subunit PP1A decreases during neural crest specification in vitro at times when TCOF1 and NOLC1 engage CUL3KBTBD8 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by expression analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Monoubiquitylation by CUL3KBTBD8 allows NOLC1 and TCOF1 to bind each other and recruit enzymes required for ribosome biogenesis and neural crest specification.
source: Monoubiquitylation by CUL3KBTBD8 allows NOLC1 and TCOF1 to bind each other and recruit enzymes required for ribosome biogenesis and neural crest specification (Werner et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Loss of CK2 prevents the CUL3KBTBD8-dependent assembly of the TCOF1-NOLC1 platform.
source: Loss of CK2 prevented the CUL3KBTBD8-dependent assembly of the TCOF1-NOLC1 platform to the same extent as inactivation of KBTBD8 through mutation of its CUL3-binding motif (KBTBD8Y74A) (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A comparing CK2 inhibition to KBTBD8 mutation.

claim: Depletion of CK2β or small molecule inhibition of CK2 kinase activity interferes with neural crest specification.
source: Accordingly, depletion of CK2β or small molecule inhibition of CK2 kinase activity interfered with neural crest specification (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2B-D using shRNA depletion and small molecule inhibition.

claim: hESCs that fail to produce neural crest cells induce a compensatory pathway characterized by increased expression of forebrain markers FOXG1 and SIX3.
source: We had previously shown that hESCs that fail to produce neural crest cells induce a compensatory pathway characterized by increased expression of forebrain markers, FOXG1 and SIX3 (Werner et al., 2015), and we observed the same response if hESCs were subjected to differentiation in the absence of CK2 (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work and confirmed by current data in Figure 2C.

claim: Low concentrations of the PP1 and PP2A inhibitor okadaic acid increase the efficiency of neural crest specification.
source: By contrast, low concentrations of the PP1 and PP2A inhibitor okadaic acid increased the efficiency of neural crest specification (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: CK2 is required for the recognition and monoubiquitylation of TCOF1 and NOLC1 by CUL3KBTBD8, formation of a TCOF1-NOLC1 ribosome biogenesis platform, and neural crest specification.
source: We conclude that CK2 is required for the recognition and monoubiquitylation of TCOF1 and NOLC1 by CUL3KBTBD8, formation of a TCOF1-NOLC1 ribosome biogenesis platform, and neural crest specification.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: KBTBD8 contains a highly conserved positively charged loop in proximity of Trp579.
source: By investigating sequence conservation among 54 vertebrate KBTBD8 homologs, we found a highly conserved positively charged loop that was in proximity of Trp579 (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1), a residue that is known to be required for substrate binding by CUL3KBTBD8 (Werner et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence conservation analysis shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Trp579 is required for substrate binding by CUL3KBTBD8.
source: By investigating sequence conservation among 54 vertebrate KBTBD8 homologs, we found a highly conserved positively charged loop that was in proximity of Trp579 (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1), a residue that is known to be required for substrate binding by CUL3KBTBD8 (Werner et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Mutation of the 5HK loop in KBTBD8 prevents binding to NOLC1 and TCOF1 but not to CUL3 or PKN1.
source: Replacing five His and Lys residues within this loop with Ala (KBTBD85HK) prevented binding of KBTBD8 to NOLC1 and TCOF1, whereas the interaction of KBTBD8 with CUL3 or PKN1 was not affected by this charge removal (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B using affinity-purification and western blotting.

claim: The 5HK loop of KBTBD8 is required for TCOF1 and NOLC1 ubiquitylation in cells.
source: In line with these results, KBTBD85HK was an inactive substrate adaptor that was unable to promote NOLC1 or TCOF1 ubiquitylation in cells (Figure 3D,E) and failed to induce formation of the NOLC1-TCOF1 complex (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3D and 3E using denaturing ubiquitin pulldowns.

claim: The 5HK loop of KBTBD8 is required for neural crest specification.
source: Moreover, if KBTBD85HK was the only KBTBD8 variant expressed in hESCs, cells did not differentiate into neural crest cells and instead showed the compensatory induction of the forebrain markers FOXG1 and SIX3 upon neural conversion (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3G and 3H using KBTBD8 depletion and reconstitution experiments.

claim: TCOF1 and NOLC1 fragments containing two CK2 consensus motifs are efficiently phosphorylated by the CK2α/β holoenzyme in vitro.
source: As evidenced by a CK2- and ATP-dependent increase in molecular weight, these proteins were efficiently phosphorylated by the CK2α/β holoenzyme in vitro (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A demonstrating molecular weight shifts upon CK2 phosphorylation.

claim: KBTBD8 selectively binds phosphorylated, but not unmodified, TCOF1 and NOLC1.
source: Importantly, when we then incubated purified KBTBD8 with either unmodified or phosphorylated TCOF1 or NOLC1, we found that KBTBD8 selectively bound the phosphorylated, but not unmodified, targets (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figures 4B and 4C.

claim: KBTBD8 does not recognize phosphorylated substrates if its Trp579 or the 5HK-patch are mutated.
source: KBTBD8 did not recognize phosphorylated substrates if its Trp579 or the positively charged 5HK-patch were mutated (Figure 4B,C), and KBTBD8 also did not bind a TCOF1 fragment, whose CK2 motif was destroyed by introduction of positively charged Arg residues or mutation of seven phosphoacceptor Ser residues (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4B, 4C, and 4D using mutant KBTBD8 variants.

claim: KBTBD8 binds a single phosphorylated CK2 motif with a KD of approximately 1.4 μM.
source: Titration experiments relying on fluorescence polarization revealed that KBTBD8 bound a single phosphorylated CK2 motif with a KD of ~1.4 μM, while we did not detect any interaction with an unphosphorylated TCOF1 peptide (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence polarization data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: A monomeric variant of KBTBD8 binds the phosphorylated CK2 motif with similar affinity as wildtype dimeric KBTBD8.
source: A monomeric variant of KBTBD8, in which residues at the BTB interface were mutated to prevent adaptor dimerization (Zhuang et al., 2009), bound the phosphorylated CK2 motif with a similar affinity as the wildtype dimeric KBTBD8 (Figure 4E), whereas mutation of its positively charged surface (KBTBD85HK) or competition with a negatively charged molecule known to interfere with CK2 substrate recognition, IP6, prevented substrate binding by KBTBD8 (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence polarization data shown in Figure 4E and a citation describing the monomeric variant.

claim: Phosphorylation by CK2 marks TCOF1 and NOLC1 for recognition and monoubiquitylation by CUL3KBTBD8.
source: We conclude that phosphorylation by CK2 marks TCOF1 and NOLC1 for recognition and monoubiquitylation by CUL3KBTBD8.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results including in vitro phosphorylation, binding, and ubiquitylation assays.

claim: TCOF1 and NOLC1 each have more than 10 CK2 motifs embedded in the central acidic domain of low structural complexity.
source: Consistent with this, we noticed that TCOF1 and NOLC1 each have more than 10 CK2 motifs that are embedded in the central acidic domain of low structural complexity (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: KBTBD8 associates with 10 CK2 motifs in TCOF1 and nine counterparts in NOLC1 in a CK2-dependent manner.
source: We found that KBTBD8 associated in a CK2-dependent manner with 10 CK2 motifs in TCOF1 and nine counterparts in NOLC1 (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 5B testing 24 distinct CK2 repeats.

claim: TCOF1 is monoubiquitylated on distinct Lys residues that are in close proximity to nine different phosphorylated CK2 motifs.
source: These results were supported by cellular studies: TCOF1 was monoubiquitylated on distinct Lys residues that were in close proximity to nine different phosphorylated CK2 motifs (Figure 5C) (Bian et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5C and a citation to published work.

claim: The more CK2 sites included in TCOF1, the better it binds KBTBD8.
source: Supporting these models, we found in a competition assay that the more CK2 sites were included in TCOF1, the better it bound KBTBD8 (Figure 5D,E; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by competition assay data shown in Figures 5D, 5E, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: KBTBD8 requires dimerization for target recognition at substrate concentrations below the KD of a single CK2 motif.
source: When tested at substrate concentrations below the KD of a single CK2 motif, KBTBD8 only bound fragments with multiple CK2 motifs even in the absence of competition (Figure 5G). Under these conditions, KBTBD8 required dimerization for target recognition (Figure 5G), which was also seen with KBTBD8 immunoprecipitated from cells (Figure 5H), as well as in in vitro ubiquitylation assays (Figure 4I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5G, 5H, and 4I comparing wildtype and monomeric KBTBD8.

claim: Increasing the number of E3-binding sites does not alter the nature of ubiquitylation, and TCOF1 with eight CK2 motifs is still only monoubiquitylated by CUL3KBTBD8.
source: In contrast to the effects on affinity, increasing the number of E3-binding sites did not alter the nature of ubiquitylation, and a TCOF1-fragment with eight CK2 motifs was still only monoubiquitylated by CUL3KBTBD8 (Figure 5I).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro ubiquitylation assay data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Multisite dependency allows cells to translate small increases in kinase levels or activity into large changes in signaling output.
source: Multisite dependency allows cells to translate small increases in the levels or activity of a kinase into large changes in signaling output (Csizmok et al., 2016; Gunawardena, 2005), which can introduce ultrasensitivity needed for switch-like differentiation (Serber and Ferrell, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work on multisite dependency and ultrasensitivity.

claim: In the presence of a competitor, TCOF1 with eight CK2 motifs is only able to bind KBTBD8 at high CK2 levels.
source: Notably, we found that in the presence of the competitor, TCOF1 was only able to bind KBTBD8 at high CK2 levels, where the affinity gain provided by eight phosphorylated CK2 motifs overcame the concentration advantage of the competitor (Figure 5J).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5J using CK2 titration in the presence of competitor.

claim: The Hill coefficient of the TCOF1-KBTBD8 binding reaction increases from approximately 1 in the absence of a competitor to approximately 3.5 in its presence.
source: Accordingly, the Hill coefficient of the TCOF1-KBTBD8 binding reaction increased from ~1 in the absence of a competitor to ~3.5 in its presence, which is indicative of ultrasensitive behavior.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of binding data, with the Hill coefficient indicating ultrasensitivity.

claim: A single CK2 motif is not sufficient for NOLC1 recognition by CUL3KBTBD8 in cells.
source: Contrary to the wildtype protein, NOLC1CK1 failed to bind endogenous KBTBD8 either in 293 T cells or in differentiating hESCs (Figure 6A,B). Thus, although a single CK2 motif can mediate binding of NOLC1 to KBTBD8 in vitro (Figure 5B), it is not sufficient to mediate its CUL3KBTBD8-recognition in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6A and 6B comparing wildtype NOLC1 to NOLC1CK1.

claim: Multiple CK2 repeats are required for an interaction between NOLC1 and KBTBD8, and wild-type NOLC1 with 10 CK2 motifs shows the strongest binding to KBTBD8.
source: Upon analyzing the behavior of these variants toward endogenous or overexpressed KBTBD8, we found that multiple CK2 repeats were required for an interaction between NOLC1 and KBTBD8, and wild-type NOLC1 with 10 CK2 motifs showed the strongest binding to KBTBD8 (Figure 6C,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6C and 6E testing NOLC1 variants with different numbers of CK2 motifs.

claim: CUL3KBTBD8-dependent monoubiquitylation of NOLC1 and its ubiquitin-dependent association with TCOF1 require multiple CK2 motifs.
source: In line with these results, we found that CUL3KBTBD8-dependent monoubiquitylation of NOLC1 and its ubiquitin-dependent association with TCOF1 required multiple CK2 motifs, and the most robust signaling was again observed in the presence of all phosphorylation sites (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6D and 6E using ubiquitylation assays and co-immunoprecipitation.

claim: NOLC1 variants with five or less CK2 motifs are ubiquitylated by an E3 ligase distinct from KBTBD8.
source: Interestingly, NOLC1 variants with five or less CK2 motifs were ubiquitylated by an E3 ligase distinct from KBTBD8 (Figure 6D), which did not promote TCOF1-NOLC1 complex formation and has an unknown function (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6D and 6E demonstrating KBTBD8-independent ubiquitylation.

claim: Only NOLC1 variants containing seven or more CK2 motifs are able to support neural crest specification.
source: When we introduced NOLC1 variants with increasing numbers of CK2 sites, we found that only those containing seven or more CK2 motifs were able to support neural crest specification (Figure 7A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7A-D using NOLC1 depletion and reconstitution experiments in hESCs.

claim: Wild-type NOLC1 containing all ten CK2 sites is most efficient in driving neural crest specification.
source: As seen with KBTBD8 binding and formation of the NOLC1-TCOF1 platform, wild-type NOLC1 containing all ten CK2 sites was most efficient in driving neural crest specification.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of NOLC1 variants with different numbers of CK2 motifs in neural crest specification assays.

claim: Multisite-dependency of CUL3KBTBD8 governs monoubiquitylation-dependent neural crest specification.
source: We conclude that multisite-dependency of CUL3KBTBD8 governs monoubiquitylation-dependent neural crest specification, a switch-like change in cell fate.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results showing the requirement of multiple CK2 motifs for neural crest specification.

claim: CUL3 plays a central role in metazoan development.
source: The central role of CUL3 in metazoan development (McGourty et al., 2016; Singer et al., 1999; Werner et al., 2015), and its frequent misregulation in cancer, autism, or hypertension (Hayward et al., 2017; Northcott et al., 2017; Rape, 2018), implies that this E3 ligase needs to be under strict control.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: CUL3 is frequently misregulated in cancer, autism, or hypertension.
source: The central role of CUL3 in metazoan development (McGourty et al., 2016; Singer et al., 1999; Werner et al., 2015), and its frequent misregulation in cancer, autism, or hypertension (Hayward et al., 2017; Northcott et al., 2017; Rape, 2018), implies that this E3 ligase needs to be under strict control.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: CUL3KEAP1 constitutively ubiquitylates the transcription factor NRF2 until this reaction is prevented upon cysteine modification of KEAP1 during oxidative stress.
source: Providing a first mechanism of regulation, CUL3KEAP1 constitutively ubiquitylates the transcription factor NRF2, until this reaction is prevented upon cysteine modification of KEAP1 during oxidative stress (Furukawa and Xiong, 2005; Tong et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work.

claim: CUL3KLHL12 regulates COPII vesicle size only after calcium has been released from the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: Conversely, CUL3KLHL12 regulates COPII vesicle size only after calcium has been released from the endoplasmic reticulum (McGourty et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Phosphorylation is a common event in promoting substrate recognition by SCF E3 ligases.
source: While phosphorylation is a common event in promoting substrate recognition by SCF E3 ligases (Skaar et al., 2013), this example shows that similar regulation exists for the CUL3 family of E3 ligases.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Most CK2 motifs in TCOF1 and NOLC1 are phosphorylated in cells.
source: Proteomic approaches found most of these CK2 motifs to be phosphorylated in cells (Bian et al., 2013), which we confirmed in our own experiments.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published proteomic work and confirmed by the authors' own experiments.

claim: Nine distinct monoubiquitylation sites on TCOF1 are always in proximity to CK2 motifs.
source: The CK2 motifs are spread throughout the central disordered domains of TCOF1 and NOLC1, and accordingly, we detected nine distinct monoubiquitylation sites on TCOF1 that were always in proximity to CK2 motifs.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data identifying ubiquitylation sites on TCOF1.

claim: The affinity of KBTBD8 for most CK2 motifs in TCOF1 or NOLC1 is similar to that of the E3 ligases SCFCDC4 or UBR1 to their targets.
source: KBTBD8 therefore binds more than 10 distinct motifs in TCOF1 or NOLC1 with an affinity that is akin to that of the E3 ligases SCFCDC4 or UBR1 to their targets (Csizmok et al., 2017; Tasaki et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to published affinity measurements for other E3 ligases.

claim: Hundreds of proteins compete for access to CK2 in cells.
source: However, a single CK2 motif was not sufficient for substrate binding by CUL3KBTBD8 in cells, where hundreds of proteins compete for access to CK2 (Bian et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published proteomic work.

claim: The yeast CDK inhibitor SIC1 requires approximately 5-6 phosphorylation events for recognition by the E3 ligase SCFCDC4.
source: Our results are reminiscent of the yeast CDK inhibitor SIC1, whose recognition by the E3 ligase SCFCDC4 requires ~5–6 phosphorylation events (Csizmok et al., 2017; Nash et al., 2001; Tang et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work on SIC1.

claim: Multiple E3 binding sites allow the intrinsically disordered SIC1 to rapidly rebind SCFCDC4 after a single motif dissociated, a mechanism referred to as allovalency.
source: In a mechanism referred to as allovalency, its multiple E3 binding sites allow the intrinsically disordered SIC1 to rapidly rebind SCFCDC4 after a single motif dissociated.
evidence: The claim describes a known mechanism from the literature on SIC1.

claim: TCOF1 and NOLC1 have multiple E3 binding motifs embedded in an acidic domain of intrinsic disorder.
source: Similar to SIC1, TCOF1 and NOLC1 have multiple E3 binding motifs that are embedded in an acidic domain of intrinsic disorder (IDRs).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis and comparison to SIC1.

claim: TCOF1 and NOLC1 contain a positively charged carboxy-terminal IDR with nuclear and nucleolar localization signals.
source: TCOF1 and NOLC1, however, differ from SIC1 in that they contain a positively charged carboxy-terminal IDR with nuclear and nucleolar localization signals.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis of TCOF1 and NOLC1.

claim: Ampholytic IDRs, such as TCOF1 or NOLC1, adopt a compact globular conformation that can undergo rapid structural fluctuations.
source: Biophysical work suggested that ampholytic IDRs, such as TCOF1 or NOLC1, adopt a compact globular conformation that can undergo rapid structural fluctuations (Das and Pappu, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published biophysical work.

claim: Multisite dependency of an E3 ligase provides a mechanism to control the activity of intrinsically disordered proteins.
source: We propose that multisite dependency of an E3 ligase provides an elegant mechanism to control the activity of intrinsically disordered proteins, which have now been linked to many important cell behaviors (Shin and Brangwynne, 2017).
evidence: The claim is a proposal based on the experimental findings and supported by a citation linking IDRs to cell behaviors.

claim: Ubiquitin-binding domains have not been identified in TCOF1, NOLC1, or their interaction partners.
source: It is difficult to rationalize ubiquitylation events that are agnostic to a particular Lys residue with binding of effector proteins that typically recognize both ubiquitin and a proximal substrate motif (Husnjak and Dikic, 2012), and indeed, ubiquitin-binding domains have not yet been identified in TCOF1, NOLC1, or their interaction partners.
evidence: The claim is based on the absence of identified ubiquitin-binding domains in these proteins.

claim: Mutations in TCOF1 account for approximately 90% of cases of Treacher Collins Syndrome.
source: Underscoring the importance of this regulatory circuit for human biology, mutations in TCOF1 account for ~90% of cases of the craniofacial disease Treacher Collins Syndrome (The Treacher Collins Syndrome Colla, 1996; Jones et al., 2008), while additional transcription factor binding sites in the promoter of KBTBD8 drive melanoma, a cancer of neural crest origin (Hayward et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work on Treacher Collins Syndrome.

claim: Additional transcription factor binding sites in the promoter of KBTBD8 drive melanoma.
source: Underscoring the importance of this regulatory circuit for human biology, mutations in TCOF1 account for ~90% of cases of the craniofacial disease Treacher Collins Syndrome (The Treacher Collins Syndrome Colla, 1996; Jones et al., 2008), while additional transcription factor binding sites in the promoter of KBTBD8 drive melanoma, a cancer of neural crest origin (Hayward et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published work on melanoma.

claim: Mutations in TCOF1 map throughout the IDR and typically lead to a truncated protein that has fewer phosphorylation sites.
source: The mutations in TCOF1 map throughout the IDR and typically lead to a truncated protein that has fewer phosphorylation sites and hence is less likely to engage in multisite phosphorylation and monoubiquitylation.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of TCOF1 mutations in Treacher Collins Syndrome.

claim: TCOF1 mutations in Treacher Collins Syndrome delete carboxy-terminal nuclear and nucleolar localization sequences.
source: These mutations also delete carboxy-terminal nuclear and nucleolar localization sequences (Isaac et al., 2000), and thus, additionally disrupt targeting of TCOF1 to the nucleolus.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Treacher Collins Syndrome is characterized by an environmental component that strongly affects the phenotypic strength of identical TCOF1 mutations across patients.
source: Treacher Collins Syndrome is further characterized by an environmental component that strongly affects the phenotypic strength of identical TCOF1 mutations across patients.
evidence: The claim is based on clinical observations of Treacher Collins Syndrome.

claim: CUL3KBTBD8 drives neural crest specification by catalyzing the monoubiquitylation of TCOF1 and NOLC1.
source: CUL3KBTBD8 drives neural crest specification by catalyzing the monoubiquitylation of TCOF1 and NOLC1 (Werner et al., 2015), but how it selects its targets at the right time during development is not known.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Substrate recognition by cullin-RING ligases often requires posttranslational modifications or co-adaptor proteins.
source: As substrate recognition by cullin-RING ligases often requires posttranslational modifications or co-adaptor proteins (McGourty et al., 2016; Skaar et al., 2013), we speculated that regulators of CUL3KBTBD8 could be identified as shared interactors of NOLC1 and TCOF1.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Expression of CK2 gradually increases during embryogenesis at times of neural crest development.
source: Expression of CK2 gradually increases during embryogenesis at times of neural crest development (Mestres et al., 1994), and CK2 activity had been detected in the branchial arches that are important for craniofacial bone development (Jones et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work.

claim: CK2 activity has been detected in the branchial arches that are important for craniofacial bone development.
source: Expression of CK2 gradually increases during embryogenesis at times of neural crest development (Mestres et al., 1994), and CK2 activity had been detected in the branchial arches that are important for craniofacial bone development (Jones et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: CUL3KBTBD8 is essential for establishing neural crest cells but not required for the maintenance of pluripotent stem cells.
source: While CUL3KBTBD8 is essential for establishing neural crest cells, it is not required for the maintenance of pluripotent stem cells (Werner et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Monoubiquitylation often recruits effector proteins to a modified target.
source: How monoubiquitylation by CUL3KBTBD8 helps TCOF1 and NOLC1 bind each other is also unclear: while monoubiquitylation often recruits effector proteins to a modified target (Dikic et al., 2009; Yau and Rape, 2016), no ubiquitin-binding domains have been identified in TCOF1, NOLC1, or their known binding partners.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work.

claim: TCOF1 and NOLC1 contain large stretches of acidic residues that are predicted to be of low structural complexity.
source: Indeed, rather than being organized into structural domains that engage in distinct interactions, TCOF1 and NOLC1 contain large stretches of acidic residues that are predicted to be of low structural complexity (Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published work on protein structure prediction.

claim: Metazoan development depends on tightly regulated gene expression programs that instruct progenitor cells to adopt specialized fates.
source: Metazoan development depends on tightly regulated gene expression programs that instruct progenitor cells to adopt specialized fates.
evidence: The claim is a general statement about developmental biology supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Posttranslational modifications, such as monoubiquitylation, can determine cell fate independently of effects on transcription.
source: Recent work found that posttranslational modifications, such as monoubiquitylation, can determine cell fate also independently of effects on transcription, yet how monoubiquitylation is implemented during development is poorly understood.
evidence: The claim is based on recent work in the field, though specific citations are not provided in this sentence.

claim: Monoubiquitylation plays a critical role during craniofacial development.
source: Monoubiquitylation plays a critical role during craniofacial development (Jin et al., 2012; McGourty et al., 2016; Werner et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Neural crest cells originate at the border of the neural plate and non-neural ectoderm and migrate to various target tissues in a developing organism.
source: This process begins with the emergence of neural crest cells, which originate at the border of the neural plate and non-neural ectoderm and migrate to various target tissues in a developing organism (Betancur et al., 2010; Simões-Costa and Bronner, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work on neural crest development.

claim: Neural crest cells differentiate into various derivatives, including chondrocytes, melanocytes, or glial cells.
source: Upon reaching their destination, neural crest cells differentiate into various derivatives, including chondrocytes, melanocytes, or glial cells.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of neural crest cell differentiation.

claim: Cranial neural crest cells emerge at the rostral end of the neural tube, migrate to the branchial arches, and differentiate into chondrocytes.
source: Cranial neural crest cells emerge at the rostral end of the neural tube, migrate to the branchial arches of the developing head, and differentiate into chondrocytes that lay out a collagen matrix for subsequent bone formation.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of cranial neural crest development.

claim: Misregulation of cranial neural crest specification or differentiation results in pathologies characterized by aberrant formation of craniofacial bone.
source: Accordingly, the misregulation of cranial neural crest specification or differentiation results in pathologies that are characterized by the aberrant formation of craniofacial bone (Achilleos and Trainor, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Generation of neural crest cells relies on the E3 ligase CUL3 and its substrate adaptor KBTBD8.
source: Generation of neural crest cells relies on the E3 ligase CUL3 and its substrate adaptor KBTBD8 (Werner et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: CUL3KBTBD8 monoubiquitylates TCOF1 and NOLC1, allowing them to associate with each other and recruit enzymes of ribosome biogenesis and modification.
source: CUL3KBTBD8 monoubiquitylates the RNA-binding proteins TCOF1 and NOLC1, which allows these paralogs to associate with each other and recruit enzymes of ribosome biogenesis and modification.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' previous work, as indicated by the context.

claim: Production of new and possibly modified ribosomes reshapes the mRNA translation landscape of stem cells in favor of neural crest specification.
source: The subsequent production of new and possibly modified ribosomes reshapes the mRNA translation landscape of stem cells in favor of neural crest specification (Werner et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: At later stages of craniofacial development, CUL3 pairs with KLHL12 to monoubiquitylate a COPII vesicle coat protein and accelerate collagen secretion.
source: At later stages of craniofacial development, CUL3 pairs up with a distinct adaptor, KLHL12, to monoubiquitylate a COPII vesicle coat protein and accelerate collagen secretion (Jin et al., 2012; McGourty et al., 2016), and mutations in this pathway lead to the craniofacial disorder cranio-lenticulo-sutural dysplasia (Boyadjiev et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Most differentiation events are switch-like and instruct progenitor cells to decisively adopt a more specialized fate.
source: Most differentiation events are switch-like and instruct progenitor cells to decisively adopt a more specialized fate.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of developmental biology.

claim: Self-reinforcing circuits built around transcription factors or chromatin modifiers help establish the switch-like character of differentiation reactions.
source: Epigenetic and transcriptional control have long been known to drive differentiation, and self-reinforcing circuits built around transcription factors or chromatin modifiers help establish the switch-like character of these reactions (Atlasi and Stunnenberg, 2017; Pijnappel et al., 2013).
